name: Norclostebol

lead: Norclostebol is a chlorinated derivative of nandrolone, described in 1957 and sold under names such as Lentabol. Physique readers mention it for its anabolic class, reported as strongly anabolic and weakly androgenic.

Wikipedia lists no medical uses. Its acetate ester was reported on the European black market in the late 1990s, and the main published work concerns detecting its illegal use in cattle, including a 2006 study of urinary metabolites. No human studies of muscle or appearance exist.

paras: It has no listed medical use and no established routine.
No human safety studies were found.

angle.text: Norclostebol is a chlorinated nandrolone derivative described in 1957 and reported as strongly anabolic and weakly androgenic, which is why physique readers mention it. It has no listed medical use, and published work mostly concerns detecting it in cattle.

lead: Norclostebol (4-chloro-19-nortestosterone) is a synthetic anabolic-androgenic steroid (AAS) with no current medical use. Wikipedia describes it as a chlorinated derivative of nandrolone, sold historically under names such as Lentabol, with an acetate ester sold as Anabol 4-19, and notes it was described in the literature in 1957.[1] Like other AAS, it acts as an androgen receptor agonist, and its appeal in bodybuilding contexts is the chain of androgen receptor activation, more muscle protein building and a more muscular physique.[1]

Wikipedia gives relative potency figures of about 6.6 times the anabolic and 40 percent of the androgenic potency of testosterone, and compares it with testosterone propionate at about 112 percent anabolic and 20 to 25 percent androgenic, while noting that such comparisons may not be valid and rest on limited sourcing.[1]

The main published research concerns detection. Norclostebol acetate was identified on the European black market in the late 1990s for possible use in breeding animals, and a 2006 study identified its urinary metabolites in cattle.[2] It is named on anti-doping and US federal lists of prohibited anabolic steroids and appears in drug-testing panels discussed on fitness forums.[3][4]

paras: Wikipedia lists norclostebol as an androgen receptor agonist and reports it as strongly anabolic with weaker androgenic activity, estimating about 6.6 times the anabolic and 40 percent of the androgenic potency of testosterone, while noting such comparisons may not be valid.[1] It calls it a potent anabolic with a minimal tendency toward side effects, a claim not sourced to clinical data.[1]

Norclostebol is closely related to clostebol (4-chlorotestosterone), a testosterone-derived steroid sold as an ester and as a topical wound-healing product in some countries such as Italy.[5] Clostebol is banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency and became widely known through athlete cases, including tennis player Jannik Sinner's 2024 positive tests, which the International Tennis Integrity Agency attributed to contamination from a physiotherapist's use of a topical product.[5]

After oral and subcutaneous administration to cattle, the main urinary metabolites were mainly reduced forms, detectable for one week after oral dosing and at least three weeks after injection, allowing identification of illegal use in animals.[2]

Norclostebol is named in lists of banned anabolic steroids, including the text of the US federal steroid control legislation and the NFL banned-substances list quoted in T Nation threads, and a norclostebol metabolite appears on an overseas employer urine-test panel quoted there.[3][4][6][7]
No studies found in humans. The published literature consists of a 2006 study of its metabolites in cattle urine.[2]
